name: Survodutide
lead: Survodutide (BI 456906) is an investigational once-weekly injectable peptide that activates both the glucagon receptor and the GLP-1 receptor. It is being developed by Boehringer Ingelheim for obesity, type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and has not been approved as a medicine at the time of writing.[1][2][3][4] For appearance, the relevant effect is reduction of body weight and liver fat: in trials, participants lost a double-digit percentage of body weight, which is the route by which interest in the drug reaches leaner-physique goals.[8][7]

Its logic is that adding glucagon-receptor activation, which is thought to raise energy expenditure and act on the liver, may produce more weight loss than GLP-1 receptor agonism alone.[1][5] Reviews group it with retatrutide and mazdutide among glucagon/GLP-1 co-agonists.[1][5]

Phase 2 trials reported weight loss, improved blood sugar and liver histology benefits, and phase 3 results in obesity and in obesity with fatty liver disease were published in 2026.[6][7][8][9][19] The evidence relates to medical weight management in people with obesity or liver disease rather than cosmetic use, and no community discussion of it for appearance was available for this entry.
infobox: Dual glucagon receptor / GLP-1 receptor agonist

paras: Survodutide is under study for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, and for MASH and MASLD.[6][8][9][10][11] Registered phase 3 trials include the SYNCHRONIZE programme in obesity, a study in adults with cirrhosis due to MASH, studies in type 2 diabetes, and a study in women through or after menopause.[12][13][14][15]

Glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying, and the later generation of agents engages additional gut hormone receptors. A 2026 Endocrine Reviews article describes the newer agents as engaging receptors for GIP, glucagon, amylin and peptide YY to enhance energy uptake, storage and expenditure through synergistic mechanisms, and lists survodutide and mazdutide as glucagon co-agonists that have shown significant weight loss and improved glycaemic control.[5] Dual glucagon and GLP-1 receptor agonism was hypothesised in the MASH trial to be potentially more effective than GLP-1 agonism alone for liver disease.[6]

Obesity (phase 2): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding trial at 43 centres in 12 countries enrolled 387 adults aged 18 to 75 with BMI of 27 or above and no diabetes, with treatment over 46 weeks. Mean bodyweight change at week 46 ranged from -6.2% in the lowest-dose group to -14.9% in the highest, compared with -2.8% on placebo; 60 percent completed treatment. Adverse events occurred in 91 percent of survodutide recipients and 75 percent of placebo recipients, mainly gastrointestinal.[7]

Obesity (phase 3): SYNCHRONIZE-1 in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2026 randomised 725 adults without diabetes (mean BMI 37.9, 41 percent men) to survodutide at two target doses or placebo with lifestyle counselling. At week 76, body weight had changed by -12.2% and -13.0% in the two survodutide groups against -5.4% on placebo, and about 72 percent of survodutide participants versus 46 percent of placebo participants lost at least 5 percent.[8] SYNCHRONIZE-MASLD, in adults with obesity and fatty liver disease, was published in Nature Medicine the same year.[9] The designs of the two phase 3 obesity trials and a cardiovascular outcomes trial have been described.[10][11]

MASH: a 48-week phase 2 trial in 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and fibrosis stages F1 to F3 reported improvement in MASH without worsening of fibrosis in 47, 62 and 43 percent of the three survodutide groups versus 14 percent on placebo. A phase 1 study examined it in cirrhosis.[6][16] Reviews and a network meta-analysis include survodutide among agents showing promise for MASH resolution and fibrosis.[17][18]

Type 2 diabetes: a 16-week phase 2 trial of 413 adults on metformin compared several survodutide regimens with placebo and open-label semaglutide. HbA1c fell by about 0.9 to 1.7 percentage points across survodutide groups, and body weight fell by up to 8.7 percent versus 5.3 percent with semaglutide; adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal, were reported by 77.8 percent of survodutide recipients.[19]
These trials involve patients with obesity or liver disease. No studies found of survodutide in healthy people seeking an aesthetic change.

In the obesity and diabetes phase 2 trials, adverse events were mostly gastrointestinal and dose-related.[7][19] Safety is being assessed across the programme, including cardiovascular outcomes and tolerability. A review of GLP-1-based medicines discusses safety questions for the class, including effects on muscle strength, bone density, gastrointestinal motility and retained gastric contents.[1] Another review notes that glucagon co-agonists such as survodutide have shown significant weight loss and glycaemic improvement.[5]

Ongoing registered studies include a phase 3 trial for people with obesity without diabetes, a trial on heart structure and function in obesity with fatty liver disease, formulation comparisons for pre-filled syringes and pen injectors, and a study of energy use and fat breakdown.[20][21][22][23] A systematic review of emerging obesity drugs lists survodutide among phase 3 GLP-1/glucagon co-agonists.[2]

card.summary: A glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist in phase 3; real weight-loss trials in obesity and liver disease, not yet approved.
card.note: Investigational; evidence is in patients, not cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Survodutide is a weekly injection that activates glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. It is in phase 3 trials for obesity and liver disease, from Boehringer Ingelheim.

Phase 2 and 3 trials report weight loss in people with obesity, but it is not approved and has no cosmetic-use evidence.
quick.mechanism: GLP-1 activation reduces appetite while glucagon receptor activation is thought to raise energy expenditure and act on the liver.
quick.risks: Safety is still under evaluation in phase 3 and cardiovascular outcomes trials. As a GLP-1-class drug, questions include muscle, bone and gastrointestinal effects. It is not available as an approved medicine.
